1859-1917

Caption This

Politics, Populism, and Empire

11

How this works (15–20 minutes)

  1. Look at each of the 5 images. Read the “What you’re looking at” line.
  2. Write a short, funny caption, like a meme. Pick a caption style if you want one.
  3. Then write 2–3 sentences about what is really going on. Use at least one key term from the lesson. Type the key term in English, exactly as shown.
  4. Save Progress any time. When all 5 are done, press Finished and upload the file to Canvas.

Keep it respectful: make the joke about the company, the idea, or the situation. Never joke about workers, children, immigrants, enslaved or freed people, Native peoples, anyone’s race or religion, or people who were hurt.

Image 1 of 5

A one-cent show in the big city

Not done

What you’re looking at: A black-and-white photograph from Norton Ch. 18. A tall building has a huge arched sign that reads “Automatic One Cent Vaudeville and Crystal Hall.” Banners below it advertise shows with names like “Falsely Accused” and “The Cowboy Gambler.” A crowd of people walks by on the street.

Heads up: Real people walk by on this street. Aim your joke at the giant sign, the one-cent price, or the show titles. Never joke about the people in the crowd.

  • What does the big arch sign say? How much does it cost?
  • Who is walking by on the street?
Pick a caption style (optional)

Key terms that fit this image: Gilded Agetenements
Image 2 of 5

The Bosses of the Senate

Not done

What you’re looking at: A color cartoon from 1889 in Norton Ch. 18. Giant money bags in suits and top hats tower over the Senate. Each bag has a label like “Steel Beam Trust,” “Standard Oil Trust,” or “Sugar Trust.” A sign says “This is a Senate of the Monopolists, by the Monopolists, for the Monopolists.” Tiny senators sit at desks below them.

Heads up: This cartoon makes fun of the trusts and of how the Senate worked. Aim your joke at the giant money bags, the signs, or the closed “People’s Entrance.” Never joke about how any person looks or about any group of people.

  • Who is standing over the senators? What are the money bags labeled?
  • Which door is open? Which door is closed? Who is each one for?
Pick a caption style (optional)

Key terms that fit this image: Gilded AgeInterstate Commerce Commission (ICC) (1887)
Image 3 of 5

“I Feed You All!” poster

Not done

What you’re looking at: A colorful poster from the 1870s in Norton Ch. 18. A farmer plows with two horses in the middle. Small scenes around the edge each have a banner, like “I plead for all,” “I rule for all,” “I fight for all,” “I carry for all,” “I sail for all,” and “I fleece you all.” The big banner says “I Feed You All!”

Heads up: The farmer is the hero of this poster. Aim your joke at the big claim, the long list of banners, or the very serious horses. Never joke about farmers, poor people, or debt.

  • Who is in the middle of the poster? What is he doing?
  • Read two of the small banners. Who is “for all,” and who is “fleecing”?
Pick a caption style (optional)

Image 4 of 5

The Maine front page

Not done

What you’re looking at: The front page of the New York Journal from February 17, 1898 (Norton Ch. 19). The headlines say “$50,000 Reward. Who destroyed the Maine?” and “Destruction of the War Ship Maine was the work of an enemy.” A drawing below shows the ship on the water.

Heads up: This is a serious one. The battleship Maine exploded and sank in Havana Harbor, and 266 sailors died, Norton says. Write one clear, serious line. No jokes about the sailors, Spain, or Cubans. Look at what the newspaper is doing with the story.

  • What does the biggest headline say? Does it show proof?
  • Why would a newspaper offer a $50,000 reward?
Pick a caption style (optional)

Image 5 of 5

Roosevelt and the big stick

Not done

What you’re looking at: A color cartoon from Norton Ch. 19. A giant Theodore Roosevelt walks through the Caribbean Sea. He carries a huge club called the “big stick” and pulls a line of warships behind him. Some ships have names like “The Debt Collector,” “The Sheriff,” and “The Receiver.” Country names around the sea include Cuba, Santo Domingo, Panama, and Mexico.

Heads up: Real countries and people live around this sea. Aim your joke at the giant stick, the giant steps, or the warships with job names. Never joke about the people of the Caribbean.

  • What is the giant man carrying? What is behind him in the water?
  • Read the names on three ships. What jobs do they sound like?
